quizzes.title: Checkpoint 1 — Containers, Images, and Run Basics
quizzes.intro: Check whether you understand why containers exist and how images, containers, and basic runs relate.

questions.prompt: What problem do containers primarily help reduce?

options.text: The need for any application testing
Environment drift by packaging apps with dependencies for more consistent runs
All security vulnerabilities forever
The need to write application code

questions.explanation: Containers improve environment parity by bundling dependencies and isolating process environments.

wrongExplanations.c: Containers do not automatically secure reckless apps.
wrongExplanations.d: You still write and maintain application code.

questions.prompt: How do containers typically differ from virtual machines?

options.text: Containers always emulate full hardware with a guest OS like a heavy VM
Containers usually share the host kernel and isolate processes more lightly than full VMs
VMs cannot run any operating system
Containers and VMs are identical in every way

questions.explanation: Containers share the host kernel and are generally lighter-weight than full VMs for many app workloads.

wrongExplanations.a: That description fits VMs more than containers.
wrongExplanations.c: VMs commonly run guest operating systems.
wrongExplanations.d: They differ in isolation model and typical resource cost.

questions.prompt: What is the relationship between an image and a container?

options.text: An image is a running process; a container is a registry only
An image is a template; a container is a runnable instance created from it
They are unrelated marketing terms
A container builds an image every time it prints logs

questions.explanation: Images template containers; many containers can run from one image.

wrongExplanations.d: Logging does not redefine image builds.

questions.prompt: What does publishing a port with `-p 8080:80` generally do?

options.text: Deletes the image permanently
Maps a host port to a container port so you can reach the service
Guarantees encryption automatically
Creates a volume named 8080

questions.explanation: Port publishing creates a pathway from the host into the container’s listening port.

wrongExplanations.a: Port flags are not delete operations.
wrongExplanations.c: Publishing is not the same as securing traffic.
wrongExplanations.d: Volumes are separate from port maps.

questions.prompt: Why does a container usually stop when its main process exits?

options.text: Because Docker forbids long-running software
Because the container’s lifecycle follows its primary process
Because images cannot contain binaries
Because registries delete it instantly

questions.explanation: Containers are process-centric; when the main process ends, the container stops.

wrongExplanations.d: Registries do not delete containers on process exit.

quizzes.title: Checkpoint 2 — Dockerfiles, Volumes, and Compose
quizzes.intro: Apply Dockerfile layering, secrets hygiene, volumes, networking, and Compose basics.

questions.prompt: Why does Dockerfile instruction order matter for build speed?

options.text: Because Docker ignores caching entirely
Because layers are cached and early changes invalidate later layers
Because the first line must always be CMD
Because order changes the host CPU brand

questions.explanation: Layer caching makes putting stable steps earlier a practical performance habit.

wrongExplanations.a: Caching is central to Docker builds.
wrongExplanations.c: FROM comes first typically; CMD is later.
wrongExplanations.d: Instruction order does not change hardware identity.

questions.prompt: What belongs in `.dockerignore` for many projects?

options.text: Nothing; always send the entire disk
Local junk like `.git`, dependencies folders, and secret env files you should not bake in
The Dockerfile itself always
Only the application source you need to run

questions.explanation: Ignoring unnecessary and sensitive files shrinks context and reduces secret accidents.

wrongExplanations.a: Huge contexts slow builds and raise risk.
wrongExplanations.c: You need the Dockerfile to build.
wrongExplanations.d: You generally need to include required source, not exclude it.

questions.prompt: Why use volumes for databases in containers?

options.text: Because databases cannot run in containers otherwise ever
Because container filesystems are treated as ephemeral and data should persist beyond container lifecycle
Because volumes delete data every second
Because volumes replace the need for passwords

questions.explanation: Volumes persist data outside the container’s ephemeral writable layer expectations.

wrongExplanations.a: They can run, but data loss is the risk without persistence.

questions.prompt: On a user-defined Docker network, how do services often address each other?

options.text: Only by guessing random IPs with no names
By container/service name DNS such as talking to `db` from another service
By emailing the registry
By publishing every port to the public internet mandatorily

questions.explanation: Docker DNS on user-defined networks resolves service/container names for inter-service traffic.

wrongExplanations.a: Name resolution is a key convenience.
wrongExplanations.d: Internal services often should not be published broadly.

questions.prompt: What is Docker Compose mainly for at beginner level?

options.text: Declaring and running multi-container applications with YAML
Replacing the need for Dockerfiles forever
Mining cryptocurrency inside registries
Editing the Linux kernel automatically

questions.explanation: Compose declares services, networks, and volumes for multi-container apps.

wrongExplanations.b: You still build images, often via Dockerfiles.

quizzes.title: Final Quiz — Hygiene, Debugging, and Professional Practice
quizzes.intro: Use the full lesson. Focus on secrets, debugging, image hygiene, and durable team habits.

questions.prompt: Where should production secrets generally not go?

options.text: In approved secret managers or runtime injection patterns
Baked into Dockerfiles or public images via copied `.env` files
In orchestrator-supported secret mechanisms
In private team vaults with access control

questions.explanation: Baking secrets into images and Dockerfiles is a classic beginner disaster.

questions.prompt: An app in a container is unreachable from the host though the process seems up. A common cause is:

options.text: The app binding only to `127.0.0.1` inside the container
Using a Dockerfile at all
Naming a volume
Reading logs

questions.explanation: Inside containers, binding to localhost can block published-port access from the host; bind to `0.0.0.0` when appropriate.

wrongExplanations.b: Dockerfiles are normal and necessary for builds.
wrongExplanations.c: Volumes are unrelated to this symptom.
wrongExplanations.d: Reading logs is diagnostic, not a cause.

questions.prompt: What is a benefit of multi-stage builds?

options.text: They force you to include all build tools in the final runtime image
They let you build in one stage and copy artifacts into a smaller runtime image
They remove the need for tags
They disable logging forever

questions.explanation: Multi-stage builds shrink runtime images by leaving compilers and build tools behind.

questions.prompt: Why pin image tags like `node:20-alpine` instead of relying on `latest` in teams?

options.text: Because reproducibility suffers when `latest` drifts unexpectedly
Because Docker cannot pull numbered tags
Because alpine images cannot run Node
Because pinning disables networking

questions.explanation: Pinned tags make builds more predictable across time and machines.

wrongExplanations.b: Numbered and specific tags are normal.
wrongExplanations.c: Alpine Node images are commonly used.

questions.prompt: What should you check early when a container exits unexpectedly?

options.text: Only the stock wallpaper on your laptop
Exit status via `ps -a` style listings and the container logs
Whether Compose YAML supports poetry exclusively
If the registry can send physical mail

questions.explanation: Status plus logs are the first-line debugging tools.

questions.prompt: Which habit best reflects professional beginner Docker practice?

options.text: Hand-edit production containers as unique snowflakes and never rebuild
Commit Dockerfiles/Compose, avoid secrets in images, rebuild for lasting changes, and document run steps
Publish every port on the internet by default
Assume containers replace app security reviews

questions.explanation: Declarative files, secret hygiene, rebuild discipline, and docs are the durable path.
